0: In the previous nineteen chapters, we repeatedly saw the same thing: model capabilities are general-purpose, and what really determines whether a project succeeds is whether the scenario has been broken down clearly enough. The same 7B model may work in one pass for contract clause extraction, yet for customer service quality inspection it requires repeated adjustments to the data annotation criteria. The difference is not in the model, but in the scenario.
1: This chapter does not introduce new models; instead, it explains clearly "how to write a real scenario into a tutorial that others can reproduce." We welcome people from all industries to write down their own implementation experience, but with one prerequisite: the scenario must be a real implementation practice and must be reproducible by third parties.
2: Why a scenario library is needed
3: The most easily missing link in open-source tutorials is not the principles, but the "last mile": where the data comes from, how the annotation criteria are defined, and what to adjust first when the results are poor. This knowledge is scattered across each team's project retrospectives, and if it is not written down, it will disappear as personnel change. The value of a scenario library is to save latercomers from having to learn by trial and error from scratch.
4: There are also direct benefits for the contributors themselves: a reproducible scenario tutorial is the most persuasive technical resume; the process of being cited, reproduced, and improved will in turn expose the blind spots in one's own solution.
5: What counts as a reproducible scenario
6: We use a four-question checklist to judge. If even one of the four questions cannot be answered, the tutorial is not yet suitable for inclusion.
7: Authenticity: the problem comes from real business, not a topic artificially created to demonstrate model capabilities. De-identification is allowed, but fictional business backgrounds are not.
8: Reproducibility: provide the data source or de-identified samples, the model and version, key parameters, and the runtime environment. If readers follow along, the results should fall within a reasonable margin of error.
9: Verifiability: clearly state which metrics are used to judge good or bad, and preferably provide a baseline. "The results are good" without a baseline cannot be tested.
10: Compliance: the data is authorized and does not contain personal information, trade secrets, or illegal content; for sensitive scenarios involving faces, voiceprints, healthcare, finance, etc., the compliance boundaries need to be explained.
11: The minimal structure of a scenario tutorial
12: It does not need to be written as a paper, but the following seven sections are recommended to be complete. Keep each section to a few hundred words so that readers can judge within the time of a cup of coffee whether the tutorial applies to them.
17: Who uses it, what pain point it solves, how it is done now
18: Only write "improve efficiency", do not write the current cost
20: What the input is, what the output is, where the boundary lies
21: Turned an open-ended problem into a classification problem
23: Source, scale, annotation criteria, de-identification method
26: Model, fine-tuning or RAG, key parameters
27: Missing version numbers and inference parameters
29: Metrics, test set, baseline, confidence interval
30: Only look at accuracy on the training set
32: GPU memory, duration, and unit price for training and inference
37: Two outlines you can apply directly
38: Outline A: Document extraction. In the business background, clearly describe the document circulation steps; in the task definition, provide the field list and null-value rules; in the data section, explain how annotation consistency is accepted (e.g., double annotation plus arbitration); in the solution section, compare three routes: general models, fine-tuned models, and "rules plus model"; in the evaluation, report precision and recall per field, and separately report null-value misjudgments; split the cost into two tiers: offline batch processing and online invocation.
39: Outline B: Dialogue and Agent. In the business background, clearly describe where the dialogue sits in the business process; in the task definition, distinguish "can chat" from "can get things done," and list the callable tools and permission boundaries; in the data section, provide desensitized samples of real conversations and failure samples; in the solution section, explain the tool-calling protocol, timeouts, and retries; in the evaluation, in addition to answer quality, also report the task completion rate and the privilege-escalation rate; in the pitfalls section, focus on cases where the model "appears to have completed" but actually did not call the tool.
41: Write the tutorial in Markdown, and submit it together with desensitized samples and reproduction scripts to the content/scenarios/ directory of the repository, with the title format "Scenario name: one-sentence conclusion." Review looks at only three things: whether it can be run through according to the document, whether the metrics can be rechecked, and whether it crosses compliance boundaries. Once approved, it will be included in the scenario library, and the contributor and verification date will be noted in the body text.
42: If it is temporarily inconvenient to disclose data, you can also submit only the "method and evaluation protocol," replacing the data with synthetic samples from the same distribution. We care more about whether the method is honest than whether the data is large.
44: Only screenshots and conclusions, with no executable steps.
45: The model version is written as "latest version," so readers cannot reproduce it.
46: The evaluation set overlaps with the training set, so the metrics are inflated.
47: Treating a one-time demo result as a stable result, without multiple runs.
48: The data source is unclear, or anonymization is incomplete.
49: There are countless scenarios. What is truly scarce is not ideas, but the patience to turn an idea into something others can rerun. You are welcome to start with the scenario you are working on right now.
